title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
html:
Trees & Binary Search Trees

A tree is a graph with no cycles and one path between any two nodes. That constraint is what makes recursion the natural tool: every subtree is the same problem, smaller.

Traversals

Depth-first, three orders, differing only in when the node is visited relative to its children:

  • Pre-order (node, left, right) - copying or serialising a tree, because the root arrives first.
  • In-order (left, node, right) - on a BST this yields sorted order. That single fact is the reason in-order matters.
  • Post-order (left, right, node) - freeing or computing anything that needs children's results first, like height or subtree sums.

Breadth-first (level by level, with a queue) - anything about levels: depth, the view from one side, printing per row.

Recursive traversal is clearer; iterative with an explicit stack avoids stack overflow on a deep tree. A tree of a million nodes shaped like a list will overflow.

Binary search tree

Left subtree smaller, right subtree larger, applied recursively. Search, insert and delete are O(height).

The catch that matters: O(height), not O(log n). Those are equal only when the tree is balanced. Insert sorted data into a naive BST and every node has one child - a linked list wearing a tree's interface, O(n) per operation.

Self-balancing variants (red-black, AVL) restructure on insert to keep the height logarithmic. That is what the standard library's sorted map is, and it is why you should almost never write your own BST for production.

Delete is the awkward operation: a node with two children must be replaced by its in-order predecessor or successor. Worth writing once to understand why the other two cases are easy.

Validating a BST

The classic error is checking only left < node < right locally. That passes trees which are not BSTs, because a node deep in the left subtree may still exceed the root. The correct check carries a permitted range downward, narrowing it at each step. The lesson generalises: a local property is not a global one.

Heaps are trees too

A binary heap is a complete tree where every parent beats its children, stored in an array - children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2, no pointers needed. It gives O(1) access to the extreme and O(log n) insert and extract, and it is not sorted, only partially ordered. That weaker promise is exactly why it is cheaper than a BST.

Tries

A tree keyed by character position, for prefix work: autocomplete, dictionary membership, longest common prefix. Lookup costs O(key length) regardless of how many keys are stored - independent of n, which no hash of the whole string gives you when you need prefixes.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming a BST is balanced.
  • Validating with a local comparison instead of a range.
  • Recursing on a deep tree and overflowing the stack.
  • Reaching for BFS to compute height when a post-order recursion is three lines.
